newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia sees UN mandate extension in E.Slavonia.
newsitem.headline: Croatia sees UN mandate extension in E.Slavonia.

text.p: Croatia said on Tuesday it expected the U.N. Security Council to extend its peacekeeping mandate in Serb-held Eastern Slavonia for six months -- three months longer than Zagreb had wanted.

Speaking to reporters after meeting his Italian counterpart, Lamberto Dini, Foreign Minister Mate Granic indicated his government would not object if the U.N. chose to keep troops there until mid-July and an additional monitoring mission stayed to the end of 1997.
Earlier, Croatian officials had lobbied for a plan in which the 5,000 troops of the U.N. Transitional Administration in Eastern Slavonia (UNTAES) would start leaving by early spring.

"I informed Mr Dini that we expect the U.N. Security Council to pass a resolution this week, extending the UNTAES mandate for a maximum six months, with an additional monitoring mission in the following six months during which Croatia would take over the control of the area," Granic said.
A senior ministry official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said this effectively meant Croatia would accept last week's recommendation of Secretary General Boutro-Boutros Ghali.
The official said Granic's comments were intended to prepare the domestic ground for yet another highly unpopular extension.
"What is important for us is that we have a date when the U.N. mandate definitely ends," the official said. "What we don't want is an open-ended mandate which could be extended perennialy."
Croatian President Franjo Tudjman faces re-election in 1997 and hopes the return of the last of the three enclaves to Croatian rule would boost his chances of winning the poll.
Serb rebels captured the enclaves, collectively known as Serb Krajina, in 1991. Croat forces reclaimed two of the regions in a series of lightening offensives last year.

During their talks, Granic and Dini also signed two bilateral accords, one on the protection of ethnic minorities in both countries, and the other on the promotion and protection of bilateral investments.
A Croatian ministry official said the minorities accord was a landmark because it mentioned the Croatian minority in Italy for the first time since World War Two.
"As far as ethnic Italians in (the Croatian provinces of) Istria and Dalmatia are concerned, the agreement confirms the present situation," the official said.

Granic said he expected Italy to support Croatia in its key long-term goal of joining West European organisations, including the European Union and NATO, independently of other former Yugoslav republics.
Croatia opposes the so called "regional approach" of the EU, which makes Croatia's entry conditional upon its developing closer relations with Serbia, Bosnia and Albania.
"We are willing to develop realations with all countries in the south-eastern Europe... but what is unacceptable to us is any kind of (political) association," Granic said.
Croatian President Franjo Tudjman is also expected to receive Dini during his visit.
